邓小平.note: 1904–1997. Here a mid-ranking political officer in Yan'an; after Mao Zedong's death, China's paramount leader and the architect of its “reform and opening.”

卓琳.note: 1916–2009. Born Pu Qiongying, daughter of a wealthy Yunnan ham merchant; Deng Xiaoping's wife from 1939 to the end of his life.

罗青长.note: 1918–2014. A young Yan'an-trained intelligence officer and “living file,” aide to Zhou Enlai; later minister of the Central Investigation Department.

汪东兴.note: 1916–2015. Rose from Mao Zedong's Yan'an bodyguard to head of the Central Guard Bureau; a CCP vice-chairman in the years just after Mao's death.

许建国.note: 1903–1965. Born Du Liqing; a veteran security officer, deputy head of the Border Security and later head of the Jin-Cha-Ji Social Affairs Department. Rendered “Du Liqing” where the book uses his original name.

谭政文.note: 1910–1961. A Long March security cadre, deputy head of the Border Region Security Office; later a senior procuratorial official.

赵苍璧.note: 1916–1993. A northern-Shaanxi local cadre who rose through investigation work; minister of public security of the People's Republic from 1977 to 1983.

李启明.note: An intellectual cadre from Shanxi and son-in-law of Li Kenong; the youngest deputy head of the Border Security, later governor of Shaanxi. One of the author's interviewees.

陈龙.note: 1910–1958. From the Northeast anti-Japanese forces; Mao Zedong's guard at the Chongqing negotiations and a pioneer of Communist counter-espionage.

凌云.note: 1917–2018. A Social Affairs Department trainee; the first Minister of State Security of the People's Republic.

贺龙.note: 1896–1969. A founder of the Red Army and later a marshal of the People's Republic; died persecuted in the Cultural Revolution.

林彪.note: 1907–1971. A leading Communist general and later marshal; named Mao Zedong's successor, he died fleeing China after an alleged coup attempt.

江青.note: 1914–1991. A Shanghai film actress and Mao Zedong's fourth wife; a leader of the Cultural Revolution and a member of the “Gang of Four.”

聂荣臻.note: 1899–1992. Commander of the Jin-Cha-Ji base area behind Japanese lines and later a marshal of the People's Republic.

李宗仁.note: 1890–1969. Guangxi militarist and Nationalist general, victor at Tai'erzhuang; briefly acting president of the Republic of China, he returned to the mainland in 1965.

董必武.note: 1886–1975. A founder of the CCP; deputy head of its wartime Southern Bureau in Chongqing, and later acting head of state of the People's Republic.

叶剑英.note: 1897–1986. A Communist general and later marshal; in charge of liaison for the Southern Bureau, and decades on a decisive figure in the arrest of the Gang of Four.

李德.note: Chinese name of Otto Braun (1900–1974), the German Comintern military adviser to the CCP and the only Westerner to make the Long March.

布鲁.note: A White-area underground veteran; reconnaissance chief of the Border Security and head of its first Qilipu training class.

王炎堂.note: Born Huang Jintang; entered the Social Affairs Department at fifteen and became an expert on the Nationalist secret services; later a deputy minister of the Central Investigation Department and one of the author's interviewees.

三青团.note: The Nationalists' youth organization, founded in 1938 and folded back into the Kuomintang in 1947.

整风.note: The Yan'an Rectification, launched in 1942: Mao Zedong's campaign of ideological remolding and cadre screening.

ch02.anchor: the thirty-eighth of the Meiji era
ch02.note: The rifle was the Japanese Arisaka Type 38, adopted in the thirty-eighth year of the Meiji reign (1905); Chinese soldiers called it the “Type-38 big cover” for its sliding bolt-cover. The nickname carried over to the cadres who joined the revolution around 1938, the so-called “'38-style.”

ch02.anchor: the Whampoa Academy of Communist intelligence and security
ch02.note: The Whampoa Military Academy, founded near Guangzhou in 1924 during the first Nationalist–Communist alliance, trained the officer corps of the National Revolutionary Army; its graduates and instructors became commanders on both sides of the later civil war. To dub the Qilipu camp a “Whampoa” is to claim that prestige for the Communist security service.

ch02.anchor: his report on the Three People's Principles Youth League
ch02.note: The Three People's Principles Youth League (Sanqingtuan) was the Nationalists' youth organization, founded in 1938 to gather young people under Chiang Kai-shek's leadership and folded back into the Kuomintang in 1947.

ch02.anchor: An important leader of security work, Wang Dongxing
ch02.note: Wang Dongxing (1916–2015) rose from this beginning to run Mao Zedong's personal security for decades as head of the Central Guard Bureau, and became a CCP vice-chairman in the interregnum after Mao's death.
Ling Yun (1917–2018), a career counter-espionage officer, would become the first Minister of State Security when that ministry was created in 1983.

The Yan'an Rectification (zhengfeng), launched in 1942, was Mao Zedong's campaign to remold the Party's thinking and consolidate his leadership. Its “cadre screening” (shen'gan) phase shaded into the coercive spy-hunt of the “Rescue Campaign” (see Chapter 9).

ch02.anchor: Deng Xiaoping, too, had the matter of a wife to settle.
ch02.note: Deng Xiaoping (1904–1997), here a mid-ranking political officer just out of disgrace, would emerge after Mao Zedong's death as China's paramount leader and the architect of its “reform and opening.”

ch02.anchor: the Comintern's military adviser to the Party, Li De
ch02.note: Li De was the Chinese name of Otto Braun (1900–1974), a German Comintern agent and the only Westerner to make the Long March. As military adviser he shared the blame for the rigid positional tactics that cost the Central Soviet its base in 1934.

ch02.anchor: This Pu Qiongying was Zhuo Lin.
ch02.note: Zhuo Lin (1916–2009), born Pu Qiongying, daughter of a wealthy Yunnan ham merchant. She married Deng Xiaoping in Yan'an in 1939 and remained his wife for the rest of his life.

ch02.anchor: Mao Zedong's marriage to Jiang Qing
ch02.note: Jiang Qing (1914–1991), a Shanghai film actress who reached Yan'an in 1937 and became Mao Zedong's fourth wife. The Party leadership is said to have consented only on condition that she keep out of politics; she went on to be a chief instigator of the Cultural Revolution and a member of the “Gang of Four,” convicted after Mao's death.

ch02.anchor: read out a letter from Mao Zedong
ch02.note: The 1937 trial and execution of Huang Kegong, a decorated Red Army officer who shot a young woman for refusing him, became a celebrated demonstration of “equality before the law” in Yan'an. Mao Zedong's letter to the court, quoted here, is much reproduced; the case is well documented (CORROBORATED), though it was also put to propaganda use from the first.

ch02.anchor: Chiang Kai-shek's own book, China's Destiny
ch02.note: China's Destiny (Zhongguo zhi mingyun, 1943), a nationalist tract issued under Chiang Kai-shek's name; its attacks on “alien” ideologies were widely read as aimed at the Communists, who answered it in kind.

Li Zicheng, the northern-Shaanxi rebel whose peasant army took Beijing in 1644 and toppled the Ming, only to lose the city within weeks (see the fuller note in Chapter 1). The comparison means that this movement, unlike his, would hold what it won.

ch02.anchor: Political power grows out of the barrel of a gun
ch02.note: Mao Zedong's dictum of 1927. The author caps it with a coinage of his own — that leadership grows out of the haft of the knife, the knife being the security and police power — echoing this chapter's play on the “gun” and the “knife.”

The enlarged Politburo meeting at Zunyi in January 1935, midway through the Long March, at which Mao Zedong won effective control of the Red Army and the Party — the pivot the author treats as the start of the CCP's correction of its own course.

Wang Jingwei (1883–1944), once a leading figure of the Nationalists, went over to the Japanese and in 1940 headed a collaborationist government at Nanjing that claimed to be the true Republic of China. “Puppet” (wei) is the standard word for it on both sides of the later divide.
The Battle of Tai'erzhuang, in southern Shandong in the spring of 1938, was one of China's first major victories over the Japanese army, won by Nationalist forces under Li Zongren.

ch02.anchor: his merits always outweighed his faults
ch02.note: Deng Xiaoping's phrasing anticipates the verdict the Party would formally reach on Mao Zedong in 1981 — that his contributions outweighed his mistakes — a judgment Deng himself did much to shape.
